claim: The JAMA database captured 278,461 articles published from 1883 to 2018, representing >91% of all articles ever published there.
source: Our JAMA database captured 278,461 articles published from 1883 to 2018, representing >91% of all articles ever published there.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of articles captured and the percentage coverage of the JAMA corpus.

claim: The NEJM database captured 182,675 articles published from 1812 to 2020, which represents >99.5% of all articles ever published in NEJM.
source: Based on DOI counts, our NEJM database captured 182,675 articles published from 1812 to 2020, which represents >99.5% of all articles ever published in NEJM.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of articles captured and the percentage coverage of the NEJM corpus.

claim: The total dataset analyzed in this study was comprised of 461,136 unique articles.
source: The total dataset analyzed in this study was comprised of 461,136 unique articles.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of unique articles in the combined dataset.

claim: The use of 'the' has declined markedly over the 20th century in both JAMA and NEJM.
source: This shows a marked decline in the use of 'the' over the 20th century in both journals, a phenomenon in the general literature well known to computational linguists (Liberman, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency analysis data shown in Figure 1 and cited literature on computational linguistics.

claim: The decline in the use of 'the' over the 20th century is a phenomenon well known to computational linguists.
source: This shows a marked decline in the use of 'the' over the 20th century in both journals, a phenomenon in the general literature well known to computational linguists (Liberman, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liberman, 2016.

claim: The occurrence of specific disease terms within JAMA and NEJM reflects the changing burden of disease itself over time.
source: The occurrence of specific disease terms within JAMA and NEJM (Figure 2a and b) reflects the changing burden of disease itself over time – at least within the United States – and reflecting the interests and perspectives of authors and editors.
evidence: The claim is supported by time series data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: The occurrence of specific disease terms within JAMA and NEJM reflects the interests and perspectives of authors and editors.
source: The occurrence of specific disease terms within JAMA and NEJM (Figure 2a and b) reflects the changing burden of disease itself over time – at least within the United States – and reflecting the interests and perspectives of authors and editors.
evidence: The claim is supported by time series data shown in Figure 2a and b and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: Tuberculosis and AIDS show a marked rise and fall over decades that reflects both their impact within the United States and the attention of researchers.
source: Tuberculosis and AIDS offer perhaps more instructive examples, showing a marked rise and fall over decades that reflects both their impact within the United States and the attention of researchers.
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 2 and represents an interpretation of the patterns observed.

claim: The relative invisibility of tuberculosis and AIDS in medical literature persists as they continue on a global scale long after the development of 'magic bullets' that promised to control both infections.
source: However, this is also indicative of the relative invisibility of these two conditions, as they persist on a global scale long after the development of 'magic bullets' that promised to control both infections (McMillen, 2015; HIV/AIDS JUNPo, 2018; Keshavjee and Farmer, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McMillen, 2015; HIV/AIDS JUNPo, 2018; Keshavjee and Farmer, 2012.

claim: The emergence of concerns about ethics can be seen in the rise of words like 'ethical', 'autonomy', or 'consent'.
source: The emergence of concerns about ethics (and the rise of the field of bioethics) can be seen in the rise of words like 'ethical', 'autonomy', or 'consent' (Figure 2; Rothman, 1991; Truog, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by time series data shown in Figure 2 and citations to Rothman, 1991; Truog, 2012.

claim: Concern with 'ethical' has diminished markedly since 1995.
source: Concern with 'ethical', however, has diminished markedly since 1995, a signal worth further investigation.
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The rise of the clinical trial infrastructure and the epistemic grounding of medical science within such trials is reflected in the rise of 'controlled' and 'randomized', and still more dramatically, of 'trial' itself.
source: Even more strikingly, we see (Figure 2e and f) the rise of the clinical trial infrastructure and the epistemic grounding of medical science within such trials (Bothwell et al., 2016), reflected in the rise of 'controlled' and 'randomized', and still more dramatically, of 'trial' itself (with a corresponding decline in 'experiment').
evidence: The claim is supported by time series data shown in Figure 2e and f and a citation to Bothwell et al., 2016.

claim: There has been a corresponding decline in the use of 'experiment' as 'trial' has increased.
source: Even more strikingly, we see (Figure 2e and f) the rise of the clinical trial infrastructure and the epistemic grounding of medical science within such trials (Bothwell et al., 2016), reflected in the rise of 'controlled' and 'randomized', and still more dramatically, of 'trial' itself (with a corresponding decline in 'experiment').
evidence: The claim is supported by time series data shown in Figure 2e and f.

claim: No historian of American medicine would be surprised by the increasing focus on the hospital between 1850 and 1950.
source: No historian of American medicine would be surprised by the increasing focus on the hospital – as site of care, education, and research – between 1850 and 1950 (Rosenberg, 1987; Stevens, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rosenberg, 1987; Stevens, 1989 and represents established historical knowledge.

claim: The dramatic decline in usage of the term 'hospital' post-1950 is a surprising finding, given the presumably persisting centrality of the hospital.
source: But the dramatic decline in usage of the term, post-1950, is a surprising finding, given the presumably persisting centrality of the hospital in each of these domains.
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 2g and h and represents an unexpected observation.

claim: The passage of the Hill-Burton Act in 1946 led to the establishment of some 6800 new hospitals.
source: Did the passage of the Hill-Burton Act in 1946, which led to the establishment of some 6800 new hospitals (Health Resources and Services Administration, 1992), establish the role of hospitals in health care such that they no longer needed to be discussed and debated?
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Health Resources and Services Administration, 1992.

claim: The term 'clinic' nearly matches the rise and fall of hospital, with its peak in the 1940s.
source: The term 'clinic', however, nearly matches the rise and fall of hospital, with its peak in the 1940s.
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 2g and h.

claim: The rise and fall of 'personal equation' through bigram computation conforms well to the NEJM analysis conducted previously through examination of each instance of the term.
source: The rise and fall of 'personal equation' through the present bigram computation (Figure 3a) conforms well to the NEJM analysis conducted previously through examination of each instance of the term recognized by the NEJM's own full-text search tool (Brinkmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous analysis cited in Brinkmann et al., 2019 and data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 'Antibiotic resistance' rises with the widespread recognition of resistant bacteria in the 1950s and of their horizontal transmission of resistance in the 1960s.
source: Turning to novel searches, we see that 'antibiotic resistance' rises with the widespread recognition of resistant bacteria in the 1950s and of their horizontal transmission of resistance in the 1960s (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 3b and c and represents an interpretation of the pattern.

claim: 'Antibiotic resistance' appears to drop off in salience by the early 1980s, before a second wave of attention from the late 1980s onward.
source: It appears to drop off in salience by the early 1980s, before a second wave of attention from the late 1980s onward as it became linked to emerging infections more broadly, and concerns about the capacity of the pharmaceutical industry to keep up with such newly resistant bacteria in particular (Podolsky, 2015; Neu, 1992; Overton et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 3b and c and supported by citations to Podolsky, 2015; Neu, 1992; Overton et al., 2021.

claim: Despite the predominance in recent decades of lung cancer mortality over breast cancer mortality, 'breast cancer' is consistently mentioned at a higher rate (roughly twice the rate) than is 'lung cancer'.
source: However, despite the predominance in recent decades of lung cancer mortality over breast cancer mortality, 'breast cancer' is consistently mentioned at a higher rate (roughly twice the rate) than is 'lung cancer'.
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 3j and k.

claim: The discrepancy in mention rates between breast cancer and lung cancer parallels discrepancies seen in the ratio of National Institutes of Health funding to the burden of disease contributed by these two forms of cancer.
source: This parallels discrepancies seen in the ratio of National Institutes of Health funding to the burden of disease contributed by these two forms of cancer (Gross et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gross et al., 1999.

claim: The plot of NEJM data for 'myocardial infarction' shows a steady rise to its peak in 2000.
source: While the plot of NEJM data shows a steady rise to its peak in 2000, the plot of JAMA data shows a bimodal distribution with one peak in the 1970s, followed by a notable dip, and then a rise to a second peak in the early 2000s.
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 3l and m.

claim: The plot of JAMA data for 'myocardial infarction' shows a bimodal distribution with one peak in the 1970s, followed by a notable dip, and then a rise to a second peak in the early 2000s.
source: While the plot of NEJM data shows a steady rise to its peak in 2000, the plot of JAMA data shows a bimodal distribution with one peak in the 1970s, followed by a notable dip, and then a rise to a second peak in the early 2000s.
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 3l and m.

claim: The two peaks of occurrences of 'patent' reflect distinct sets of meaning, with patent medicines explaining the first peak and a mix of inventor's patents and congenital heart disease explaining the second peak.
source: Such an analysis answers the puzzle for 'patent' (Tables 1 and 2; Supplementary files 1 and 2): the two peaks of occurrences reflect distinct sets of meaning, with patent medicines explaining the first peak (e.g., 'patent' occurs in association with nostrum, proprietary, fakish, secret, exploiter, evil, dopers, and quackery) (Gabriel, 2014; Young, 1987), while a mix of inventor's patents (e.g., inventors, coinventors, device) and congenital heart disease (patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus) explains the second peak.
evidence: The claim is supported by word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2 and citations to Gabriel, 2014; Young, 1987.

claim: Abortion has been an enduring problem for the medical profession in the United States, with the procedure widely tolerated in the early 19th century, criminalized in the late 19th century, decriminalized in the 1970s, and contested ever since.
source: Abortion (Tables 1 and 2; Supplementary files 3 and 4) has been an enduring problem for the medical profession in the United States, with the procedure widely tolerated in the early 19th century, criminalized in the late 19th century, decriminalized in the 1970s, and contested ever since (Mohr, 1979; Reagan, 1997; De Ville, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mohr, 1979; Reagan, 1997; De Ville, 1992.

claim: 'Criminal' first appears in NEJM in the 1850s, corresponding with the medical campaign to ban abortion, and remains atop the list through the early 1900s.
source: 'Criminal' first appears in NEJM in the 1850s, corresponding with the medical campaign to ban the procedure, and remains atop the list through the early 1900s.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Contraception first appears in association with abortion in the 1930s, but does not become a strong association until the 1950s in JAMA and the 1960s in NEJM.
source: Contraception first appears in the 1930s, but does not become a strong association until the 1950s in JAMA and the 1960s in NEJM.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Legalization first appears in association with abortion in the 1970s and becomes more prominent by the 1990s.
source: Legalization first appears in the 1970s and becomes more prominent by the 1990s.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: In NEJM, religion and religious first appear in association with abortion in the 1970s, and only break into the top 10 (religious) in the 2010s.
source: In NEJM, religion and religious also first appear in the 1970s, and only break into the top 10 (religious) in the 2010s, reflecting an important observation made by historians that the abortion debate in the United States was not couched in religious terms until quite recently.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Table 2 and represents an interpretation consistent with historical scholarship.

claim: The abortion debate in the United States was not couched in religious terms until quite recently.
source: In NEJM, religion and religious also first appear in the 1970s, and only break into the top 10 (religious) in the 2010s, reflecting an important observation made by historians that the abortion debate in the United States was not couched in religious terms until quite recently.
evidence: The claim is attributed to historians and supported by the word embedding analysis.

claim: Both religion and religious are strikingly less prominent among JAMA's nearest terms for abortion – neither word falls within the top 30 associations at any point.
source: However, both religion and religious are strikingly less prominent among JAMA's nearest terms – neither word falls within the top 30 associations at any point.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Bias rose precipitously in usage, in both JAMA and NEJM, in the latter half of the 20th century.
source: Bias rose precipitously in usage, in both JAMA and NEJM, in the latter half of the 20th century (though falling, unexpectedly, in the 21st century in NEJM; Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Bias fell unexpectedly in the 21st century in NEJM.
source: Bias rose precipitously in usage, in both JAMA and NEJM, in the latter half of the 20th century (though falling, unexpectedly, in the 21st century in NEJM; Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on time series data shown in Figure 6.

claim: As of the 1920s, bias's top 20 associations are moral and vernacular.
source: As of the 1920s, its top 20 associations are moral and vernacular (Tables 1 and 2; Supplementary files 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: By the 1950s, 'uncertainty' is the #3 related term for bias in JAMA and 'subjectivity' has become the #4 related term in NEJM.
source: But we already see hints of later, less-conscious misperception, with misjudgment, denial, and subconscious included (as was 'sham') in the 1920s; and by the 1950s, 'uncertainty' is the #3 related term in JAMA and 'subjectivity' has become the #4 related term in NEJM.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: By the 1970s, bias has largely become a statistical clinical trial term.
source: By the 1970s, bias has largely become a statistical clinical trial term – with misclassification, selection, retrospective, errors, confounding, and validity all in the top 20 – but its moral associations are still apparent in such associations further down the list as unverifiable, blatantly, recalcitrance, and antisocial, demonstrating medicine's linked moral and epistemic commitments.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: A new set of associations for 'defective' rises to prominence in the early 20th century – impaired, congenitally, feebleminded, mentally, delinquents, retarded, idiot, and others – a reflection of the rise of the eugenics movement in the United States.
source: A new set of associations rises to prominence in the early 20th century (present in both JAMA and NEJM) – impaired, congenitally, feebleminded, mentally, delinquents, retarded, idiot, and others – a reflection of the rise of the eugenics movement in the United States and its concern with supposedly defective people (Kevles, 1995; Paul, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2 and supported by citations to Kevles, 1995; Paul, 1998.

claim: 'Defective' persists in modern usage, now almost exclusively in association with genes.
source: While eugenics has faded from medical discourse, 'defective' persists, now almost exclusively in association with genes (tlr1, cftr, nlrp3, dysregulated, dock2, repression, etc.).
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The persistence of 'defective' in genetics reflects the emergence of modern genetics, a very different science of inter-individual variability than that which eugenics had promised.
source: This reflects the emergence of modern genetics, a very different science of inter-individual variability than that which eugenics had promised.
evidence: The claim represents an interpretation of the word embedding data.

claim: Genetics still encodes a language of value judgments, sharing eugenics' concerns with 'defective'.
source: But genetics still encodes a language of value judgments, sharing eugenics' concerns with 'defective'.
evidence: The claim represents an interpretation of the word embedding data.

claim: The use of 'defective' in genetics will inevitably contribute to the stigmatization of genetic variations associated with diseases or other undesirable traits.
source: This will inevitably contribute to the stigmatization of genetic variations associated with diseases or other undesirable traits.
evidence: The claim represents a speculative inference about the consequences of language use.

claim: There is a longstanding debate about whether the field of medical genetics is still colored by its eugenic prehistory.
source: This is an interesting finding in the setting of the longstanding debate about whether the field of medical genetics is still colored by its eugenic prehistory (Cowan, 2008; Comfort, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cowan, 2008; Comfort, 2012.

claim: The racist aspects of medical theory and practice, from the 19th century through the 20th and into the 21st, have been well documented by historians.
source: The racist aspects of medical theory and practice, from the 19th century through the 20th and into the 21st, have been well documented by historians (Roberts, 2011; Wailoo, 2011; Braun, 2014; Vyas et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roberts, 2011; Wailoo, 2011; Braun, 2014; Vyas et al., 2020.

claim: 'Jew' and 'Negro' are especially prominent in associations with race in the eugenic decades of the early 20th century.
source: 'Jew' and 'Negro' are especially prominent in the eugenic decades of the early 20th century.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: A marked change occurs in the 1940s, when sex (and then ethnic/ethnicity) become race's closest associations.
source: A marked change occurs in the 1940s, when sex (and then ethnic/ethnicity) become race's closest associations, presumably a reflection of a shift in medical publication that linked sex and race in reporting the demographic characteristics of patients in clinical research trials (Epstein, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2 and supported by a citation to Epstein, 2008.

claim: By the 21st century, race had lost its early eccentric and eugenic associations and become an administrative category.
source: By the 21st century, race had lost (at least in these word frequency associations) its early eccentric and eugenic associations and become an administrative category (ethnic, sex, Hispanic, Asian, female, marital, etc.).
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The routinization of race as an administrative category makes a normative judgment: doctors should think race – as a biological category – is relevant.
source: This routinization has many effects. It makes a normative judgment: doctors should think race – as a biological category – is relevant.
evidence: The claim represents an interpretation of the implications of the word embedding data.

claim: The routinization of race obscures the ways in which race actually remained a contested category within medicine.
source: And it obscures the ways in which race actually remained a contested category within medicine (Tishkoff and Kidd, 2004; Pollock, 2012; Jones, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tishkoff and Kidd, 2004; Pollock, 2012; Jones, 2021.

claim: The emergence of 'self-identified' in JAMA after the 1990s reflects discomfort with what race really is.
source: One clue concerning this discomfort is reflected by the emergence of 'self-identified' in JAMA after the 1990s: unsure of what race really is, doctors increasingly defaulted to putting responsibility on patients to 'self-identify' their race, as if that made the label somehow true or safe.
evidence: The claim is based on word embedding analysis shown in Table 1 and represents an interpretation.

claim: Patients often struggle to shoehorn their complex identities into the limited options given to them for race categorization.
source: However, as many clinicians and researchers know, patients often struggle to shoehorn their complex identities into the limited options given to them (e.g., black versus nonblack, or the five races and two ethnic categories used widely in American health care).
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge among clinicians and researchers.

claim: The 1900–1924 grouping of alcoholism, dementia, and neurosyphilis reflects the fact that many of the pathological features associated with dementia were first observed in brains from individuals afflicted with general paresis and in individuals with chronic alcoholism.
source: The 1900–1924 grouping of alcoholism, dementia, and neurosyphilis – as well as its persistence into the 1925–1949 period, reflects the fact that many of the pathological features associated with dementia were first observed in brains from individuals afflicted with general paresis (due to CNS syphilitic infection) and in individuals with chronic alcoholism (Berchtold and Cotman, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on clustering analysis shown in Figure 7 and supported by a citation to Berchtold and Cotman, 1998.

claim: Samuel Wilks first described atrophy (associated with decreased brain weight) as being due to chronic alcoholism and CNS syphilis ('neurosyphilis').
source: In fact, Samuel Wilks first described atrophy (associated with decreased brain weight) as being due to chronic alcoholism and CNS syphilis ('neurosyphilis'), which was later investigated in relation to other dementias (Berchtold and Cotman, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berchtold and Cotman, 1998.

claim: The character error rate for OCR was 0.26% (± standard deviation [std] = 0.004%; 1 in 384 characters) for articles published before 1899.
source: We calculated the character error rate to be (Figure 8a): 0.26% (± standard deviation [std] = 0.004%; 1 in 384 characters) for articles published before 1899, 0.014% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 7105 characters) for articles published between 1900 and 1949, 0.065% (± std 0.002%; 1 in 1520 characters) for articles published between 1950 and 1999, and 0.037% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 2701 characters) for articles published after 2000.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific OCR error rates calculated from validation data.

claim: The character error rate for OCR was 0.014% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 7105 characters) for articles published between 1900 and 1949.
source: We calculated the character error rate to be (Figure 8a): 0.26% (± standard deviation [std] = 0.004%; 1 in 384 characters) for articles published before 1899, 0.014% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 7105 characters) for articles published between 1900 and 1949, 0.065% (± std 0.002%; 1 in 1520 characters) for articles published between 1950 and 1999, and 0.037% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 2701 characters) for articles published after 2000.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific OCR error rates calculated from validation data.

claim: The character error rate for OCR was 0.065% (± std 0.002%; 1 in 1520 characters) for articles published between 1950 and 1999.
source: We calculated the character error rate to be (Figure 8a): 0.26% (± standard deviation [std] = 0.004%; 1 in 384 characters) for articles published before 1899, 0.014% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 7105 characters) for articles published between 1900 and 1949, 0.065% (± std 0.002%; 1 in 1520 characters) for articles published between 1950 and 1999, and 0.037% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 2701 characters) for articles published after 2000.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific OCR error rates calculated from validation data.

claim: The character error rate for OCR was 0.037% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 2701 characters) for articles published after 2000.
source: We calculated the character error rate to be (Figure 8a): 0.26% (± standard deviation [std] = 0.004%; 1 in 384 characters) for articles published before 1899, 0.014% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 7105 characters) for articles published between 1900 and 1949, 0.065% (± std 0.002%; 1 in 1520 characters) for articles published between 1950 and 1999, and 0.037% (± std 0.001%; 1 in 2701 characters) for articles published after 2000.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific OCR error rates calculated from validation data.

claim: 71% of character errors occurred in digitized manuscripts published prior to the year 1899.
source: This is further validated by the observation that 71% of character errors occurred in digitized manuscripts published prior to the year 1899, with a cumulative error rate of less than 1 in 2500 in the lines published after 1900.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistics on the distribution of OCR errors.

claim: The cumulative error rate was less than 1 in 2500 in the lines published after 1900.
source: This is further validated by the observation that 71% of character errors occurred in digitized manuscripts published prior to the year 1899, with a cumulative error rate of less than 1 in 2500 in the lines published after 1900.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistics on OCR error rates.

claim: The error rate post-1900 was similar to the number of discrepancies between the two human transcribers.
source: Notably, the error rate post-1900 was similar to the number of discrepancies between the two human transcribers.
evidence: The manuscript compares OCR error rates to human transcription discrepancies.

claim: Post-2000, all OCR errors were traced back to difficulty in recognizing punctuation without a single error in alphanumeric recognition.
source: Post-2000, all OCR errors were traced back to difficulty in recognizing punctuation (e.g., long dashes) without a single error in alphanumeric recognition.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific analysis of OCR error types.

claim: All alphanumeric character discrepancies were traced back to typographical errors introduced by poor printing quality.
source: All alphanumeric character discrepancies were traced back to typographical errors introduced by poor printing quality (e.g., e recognized as c when the [horizontal] bar of the letter e is missing; Figure 8b).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific analysis of OCR error sources with examples.

claim: JAMA was founded in 1883.
source: The Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA, founded in 1883) and the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM, founded in 1812) have played critical roles in the development of medical knowledge and practice.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the founding year of JAMA.

claim: NEJM was founded in 1812.
source: The Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA, founded in 1883) and the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM, founded in 1812) have played critical roles in the development of medical knowledge and practice.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the founding year of NEJM.

claim: JAMA and NEJM have played critical roles in the development of medical knowledge and practice.
source: The Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA, founded in 1883) and the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM, founded in 1812) have played critical roles in the development of medical knowledge and practice.
evidence: The claim represents a general statement about the importance of these journals.

claim: It is difficult to analyze trends over time or perform sophisticated analyses using JAMA's and NEJM's search interfaces.
source: It is possible to do basic searches through JAMA's and NEJM's search interfaces, but it is difficult to analyze trends over time or perform more sophisticated analyses.
evidence: The claim represents an assessment of the limitations of existing search tools.

claim: PubMed and Web of Science do not capture the full 137-year history of JAMA and the 209-year history of NEJM.
source: Other online databases, notably PubMed and Web of Science, allow slightly more sophisticated searches, but neither realizes the potential of or even captures the full 137-year history of JAMA and the 209-year history of NEJM.
evidence: The claim represents an assessment of the limitations of existing databases.

claim: Progress in digital history, scientometrics, and computational linguistics has led to new approaches and techniques for the analysis of the 'big data' of medical publications.
source: Over the past decade, progress in digital history, scientometrics, and computational linguistics has led to new approaches and techniques for the analysis of the 'big data' of medical publications (Boyack et al., 2005; Börner, 2010; Jones et al., 2011; Weisz et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2016; Westergaard et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boyack et al., 2005; Börner, 2010; Jones et al., 2011; Weisz et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2016; Westergaard et al., 2018.

claim: An article is defined as any document with a digital object identifier (DOI).
source: In this study, an article is defined as any document with a digital object identifier (DOI), a system that assigns a unique identifier to academic publications.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines what constitutes an article for the purposes of the study.

claim: For the JAMA dataset, 304,905 DOIs were collected, of which 223,748 had associated authorship metadata.
source: For the JAMA dataset, we collected 304,905 DOIs, of which 223,748 had associated authorship metadata.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers for DOIs collected and those with metadata.

claim: The missing JAMA articles (<9%) have not been digitized, have erroneous DOI references that could not be corrected, or simply, were not captured during crowd-sourcing efforts.
source: The missing articles (<9%) have not been digitized, have erroneous DOI references that could not be corrected, or simply, were not captured during crowd-sourcing efforts.
evidence: The manuscript provides explanations for missing articles.

claim: The missing NEJM articles (estimated to be between 65 and 194 articles) may not have been captured for several reasons including erroneous DOIs, recent publication, or not being captured during crowd-sourcing efforts.
source: The missing articles (estimated to be between 65 and 194 articles) may not have been captured in our dataset construction for several reasons. Some of these DOIs may be erroneous and/or do not resolve to a NEJM article (estimated to be 20 articles). Alternatively, the article may have been too recent or perhaps more simply, was not captured by our volunteers during our crowd-sourcing efforts.
evidence: The manuscript provides explanations for missing articles.

claim: The missing NEJM articles represent less than 0.05–0.5% of the entire NEJM corpus and were missing at random, which would have little to no impact on subsequent analyses.
source: However, given that these articles represent less than 0.05–0.5% of the entire NEJM corpus and were missing at random, this would have little to no impact on subsequent analyses.
evidence: The manuscript provides an assessment of the impact of missing articles.

claim: OCR was performed using Tesseract v4.1.1, an open-source OCR engine using both legacy and LSTM engines and default automatic page segmentation.
source: For article PDFs that have not been digitized to machine-encoded text, we performed optical character recognition (OCR) using Tesseract v4.1.1, an open-source OCR engine using both legacy and LSTM engines and default automatic page segmentation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the OCR methodology.

claim: No pre-processing was performed prior to OCR.
source: No pre-processing was performed prior to OCR.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of pre-processing.

claim: Two individuals manually and independently transcribed the same 600 lines randomly selected from each semi-century contained in the dataset to validate the OCR results.
source: To validate the OCR results compared with the original manuscripts, two individuals manually and independently transcribed the same 600 lines randomly selected from each semi-century contained in our dataset (150 consecutive lines [composed of more than 31,000 characters] from each of the following time intervals: 1850–1899, 1900–1949, 1950–1999, 2000–2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the validation methodology.

claim: The two manually transcribed sets of lines were consolidated and manually verified by a third individual to establish the gold standard.
